questions.domain: Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning
questions.stem: A retail analytics company stores 40 TB of historical customer transaction logs in unlabeled .csv files across an Amazon S3 bucket. Several columns contain missing values, and the schema is not yet registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. An ML engineer must catalog the schema, clean and engineer features visually with minimal code, and store the prepared dataset for Amazon SageMaker training. 1. Run an AWS Glue crawler over the S3 bucket to infer schemas and populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog. 2. Run an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe job to impute missing values, apply feature encoding, and clean the dataset. 3. Write the transformed output dataset back to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format for SageMaker training. What is the correct chronological sequence of steps?
questions.explanation: First, the AWS Glue crawler inspects the raw CSV files in S3 to infer column schemas and register the table in the Glue Data Catalog (1). Second, AWS Glue DataBrew uses that cataloged dataset to run visual data cleaning and feature engineering recipes (2). Third, DataBrew outputs the cleaned dataset back to Amazon S3 in columnar Parquet format for downstream SageMaker training (3). Architectural Deep Dive: AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual, no-code data preparation service with 250+ pre-built transformations, automated data profiling, PII handling, and reusable recipes that data analysts and engineers can schedule across large S3, Redshift, and RDS datasets without writing Spark code. Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: Enterprise data governance teams use Glue DataBrew recipes to standardize date formats, mask PII columns, and impute missing values across terabytes of daily S3 CSV drops before cataloging them in the Glue Data Catalog.
questions.hack: When the stem emphasizes 'no-code visual interface', 'data profiling', or 'reusable cleaning recipes' with LEAST development effort, Glue DataBrew is your top contender.

questions.domain: Domain 4: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.stem: A company is building a web-based AI application by using Amazon SageMaker. The application will provide the following capabilities and features: ML experimentation, training, a central model registry, model deployment, and model monitoring. The application must ensure secure and isolated use of training data during the ML lifecycle. The training data is stored in Amazon S3. The company needs to use the central model registry to manage different versions of models in the application. Which action will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a separate Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository for each model.
Use Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and unique tags for each model version.
Use the SageMaker Model Registry and model groups to catalog the models.
Use the SageMaker Model Registry and unique tags for each model version.
questions.explanation: The correct choice is C: Option C (Use the SageMaker Model Registry and model groups to catalog the models.). Amazon SageMaker Model Registry provides a centralized, versioned catalog using Model Groups where each trained iteration is registered as a versioned model package with metadata, metrics, lineage, and explicit approval states (PendingManualApproval, Approved, Rejected) that integrate natively with CI/CD pipelines. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option B is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option relies on manual tag tracking or raw container repositories rather than managed model package versioning and governance workflows.
questions.use_case: In enterprise MLOps platforms, every SageMaker Pipeline run registers its candidate artifact into a Model Group as 'PendingManualApproval'; once a Lead ML Engineer approves it in Studio, an EventBridge rule automatically triggers CodePipeline to deploy the production endpoint.
questions.hack: Whenever a question combines 'central model catalog', 'manage model versions', or 'approval workflow before deployment', lock onto SageMaker Model Registry and Model Groups immediately.

options: Use Managed Spot Training.
Use SageMaker managed warm pools.
Use SageMaker Training Compiler.

questions.explanation: The correct choice is B: Option B (Use SageMaker managed warm pools.). SageMaker Managed Warm Pools retain provisioned training instances and container environments for a configurable duration (KeepAlivePeriodInSeconds) after a job finishes, slashing infrastructure provisioning and container download startup times for consecutive experimentation or iterative training runs. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: When data scientists iterate rapidly on feature subsets or consecutive training scripts in SageMaker, enabling KeepAlivePeriodInSeconds (for example, 1800 seconds) avoids waiting 4-6 minutes for EC2 provisioning and Docker image pulls on every run.
questions.hack: Spot the phrase 'consecutive training jobs' + 'minimize infrastructure startup times' -> the answer is always SageMaker Managed Warm Pools (never Spot Training, which actually adds interruption risk).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning
questions.stem: A company is building a web-based AI application by using Amazon SageMaker. The application will provide the following capabilities and features: ML experimentation, training, a central model registry, model deployment, and model monitoring. The application must ensure secure and isolated use of training data during the ML lifecycle. The training data is stored in Amazon S3. The company needs to run an on-demand workflow to monitor bias drift for models that are deployed to real-time endpoints from the application. Which action will meet this requirement?
options: Configure the application to invoke an AWS Lambda function that runs a SageMaker Clarify job.
Invoke an AWS Lambda function to pull the sagemaker-model-monitor-analyzer built-in SageMaker image.
Use AWS Glue Data Quality to monitor bias.
Use SageMaker notebooks to compare the bias.
questions.explanation: The correct choice is A: Option A (Configure the application to invoke an AWS Lambda function that runs a SageMaker Clarify job.). Amazon SageMaker Clarify computes both pre-training data bias metrics (such as Class Imbalance, DPL, KL Divergence) and post-training model bias metrics, while using Kernel SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to generate global and local feature attribution scores and monitor ongoing bias or feature attribution drift. Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option performs one-off manual notebook inspection or re-architects the pipeline instead of updating or scheduling automated SageMaker Model Monitor baselines. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: In regulated banking and healthcare ML systems, teams attach a SageMaker Clarify processing step inside SageMaker Pipelines to block any model whose Disparate Impact (DI) or SHAP feature attribution shifts beyond compliance thresholds.
questions.hack: Remember the sibling split: Clarify = Bias + Explainability (SHAP); Model Monitor = Data/Model Quality Drift in production; Debugger = Internal training tensors and gradients.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning
questions.stem: An ML engineer is developing a fraud detection model on AWS. The training dataset includes transaction logs, customer profiles, and tables from an on-premises MySQL database. The transaction logs and customer profiles are stored in Amazon S3. The dataset has a class imbalance that affects the learning of the model's algorithm. Additionally, many of the features have interdependencies. The algorithm is not capturing all the desired underlying patterns in the data. Which AWS service or feature can aggregate the data from the various data sources?
options: Amazon EMR Spark jobs
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon DynamoDB
AWS Lake Formation
questions.explanation: The correct choice is D: Option D (AWS Lake Formation). AWS Lake Formation centralizes fine-grained access control (column-level, row-level, and cell-level security) and Tag-Based Access Control (LF-TBAC) across S3 data lakes and the AWS Glue Data Catalog, while providing Blueprints to ingest data from RDS and on-premises databases. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option uses batch-only tools for streaming ingestion or deploys self-managed Kafka/Spark on raw EC2 instances when managed Kinesis, Firehose, or Glue Spark jobs meet the requirement. Option B is incorrect because this option uses batch-only tools for streaming ingestion or deploys self-managed Kafka/Spark on raw EC2 instances when managed Kinesis, Firehose, or Glue Spark jobs meet the requirement. Option C is incorrect because this option tries to use a synchronous Multi-AZ standby instance for read scaling, or uses an asynchronous Read Replica as a zero-data-loss HA failover mechanism.
questions.use_case: Multi-team analytics platforms use Lake Formation LF-Tags (such as 'Confidentiality=PII') so ML engineers automatically see only anonymized columns in Athena and SageMaker without duplicating S3 buckets.
questions.hack: Whenever you see 'centralized column/row-level security on S3/Glue' or 'aggregate data lake permissions with tags (LF-TBAC)', pick AWS Lake Formation.

questions.domain: Domain 3: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.stem: An ML engineer is developing a fraud detection model on AWS. The training dataset includes transaction logs, customer profiles, and tables from an on-premises MySQL database. The transaction logs and customer profiles are stored in Amazon S3. The dataset has a class imbalance that affects the learning of the model's algorithm. Additionally, many of the features have interdependencies. The algorithm is not capturing all the desired underlying patterns in the data. The ML engineer needs to use an Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithm to train the model. Which algorithm should the ML engineer use to meet this requirement?
options: LightGBM
Linear learner
K-means clustering
Neural Topic Model (NTM)
questions.explanation: The correct choice is A: Option A (LightGBM). For highly imbalanced datasets (such as 0.2% credit card fraud or rare disease screening), raw Accuracy is misleading because predicting the majority class yields 99.8% accuracy; instead, engineers balance data using SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) or class weights (scale_pos_weight in XGBoost) and evaluate using Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC), F1-Score, Recall (to minimize false negatives), or Precision (to minimize false positives). Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option performs risky manual endpoint swaps without automated baking periods and CloudWatch alarm auto-rollback. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: In healthcare disease screening or manufacturing safety defect detection where missing a positive case (False Negative) is catastrophic, teams optimize for Recall and use SMOTE during training.
questions.hack: Minimize False Negatives (don't miss fraud/cancer/defects) = Recall. Minimize False Positives (don't block legitimate VIP customers or spam alerts) = Precision. Balance both on imbalanced classes = F1-Score / PR-AUC.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning
questions.stem: A company has deployed an XGBoost prediction model in production to predict if a customer is likely to cancel a subscription. The company uses Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to detect deviations in the F1 score. During a baseline analysis of model quality, the company recorded a threshold for the F1 score. After several months of no change, the model's F1 score decreases significantly. What could be the reason for the reduced F1 score?
options: Concept drift occurred in the underlying customer data that was used for predictions.
The model was not sufficiently complex to capture all the patterns in the original baseline data.
The original baseline data had a data quality issue of missing values.
Incorrect ground truth labels were provided to Model Monitor during the calculation of the baseline.
questions.explanation: The correct choice is A: Option A (Concept drift occurred in the underlying customer data that was used for predictions.). Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor continuously compares live endpoint payloads and predictions against a statistical baseline (constraints.json and statistics.json) generated from the training dataset, emitting CloudWatch metrics when data drift or model quality degradation occurs. Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option performs one-off manual notebook inspection or re-architects the pipeline instead of updating or scheduling automated SageMaker Model Monitor baselines. Option C is incorrect because this option performs one-off manual notebook inspection or re-architects the pipeline instead of updating or scheduling automated SageMaker Model Monitor baselines. Option D is incorrect because this option performs one-off manual notebook inspection or re-architects the pipeline instead of updating or scheduling automated SageMaker Model Monitor baselines.
questions.use_case: When seasonal customer behavior shifts intentionally (for example, holiday retail traffic), ML engineers generate a fresh baseline dataset and update the Model Monitor MonitoringSchedule so legitimate seasonal shifts do not trigger false-positive alarms.
questions.hack: If legitimate production data distribution changes permanently, don't retrain blindly first - create a new baseline from the latest validated dataset and update Model Monitor.

questions.domain: Domain 4: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.stem: A company has a team of data scientists who use Amazon SageMaker notebook instances to test ML models. When the data scientists need new permissions, the company attaches the permissions to each individual role that was created during the creation of the SageMaker notebook instance. The company needs to centralize management of the team's permissions. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Create a single IAM role that has the necessary permissions. Attach the role to each notebook instance that the team uses.
Create a single IAM group. Add the data scientists to the group. Associate the group with each notebook instance that the team uses.
Create a single IAM user. Attach the AdministratorAccess AWS managed IAM policy to the user. Configure each notebook instance to use the IAM user.

Create a single IAM group. Add the data scientists to the group. Create an IAM role. Attach the AdministratorAccess AWS managed IAM policy to the role. Associate the role with the group. Associate the group with each notebook instance that the team uses.
questions.explanation: The correct choice is A: Option A (Create a single IAM role that has the necessary permissions. Attach the role to each notebook instance that the team uses.). For AWS security and compliance: IAM Roles with AWS STS AssumeRole provide short-lived temporary credentials for EC2, Lambda, and cross-account access (eliminating long-lived IAM User access keys); AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce central guardrails across member accounts; AWS KMS manages encryption keys (Customer Managed Keys / CMKs for custom rotation and cross-account access); AWS Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates database credentials; AWS WAF protects ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway against Layer 7 SQLi/XSS and rate-based attacks; AWS Shield protects against DDoS; Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious account/VPC/S3 threat activity using ML; and Amazon Macie discovers sensitive PII in S3 buckets. Why the distractors fail: Option B is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option embeds long-lived IAM User access keys or plaintext database passwords in code/environment variables instead of using IAM Roles and AWS Secrets Manager.
questions.use_case: Instead of creating static IAM user keys for a Lambda function in Account A to write to DynamoDB in Account B, architects create an IAM Role in Account B with a trust policy allowing Account A to call STS AssumeRole.
questions.hack: Never pick static IAM User access keys! Always choose IAM Roles + STS AssumeRole for cross-account or compute permissions, AWS Secrets Manager for automated DB password rotation, AWS WAF for Layer 7 SQLi/XSS/IP rate limiting, and Amazon Macie for finding PII in S3.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning
questions.stem: An ML engineer at a FinTech startup wants to centralize engineered credit-risk features using Amazon SageMaker Feature Store so both real-time checkout inference and offline batch model retraining use identical feature definitions. 1. Ingest streaming and batch feature records into the Feature Group using PutRecord or Data Wrangler. 2. Define and create a Feature Group schema with a record identifier and event time feature in SageMaker Feature Store. 3. Query the Offline Store via Amazon Athena to build point-in-time training datasets and query the Online Store for low-latency inference. Which sequence represents the correct implementation order?
questions.explanation: In Amazon SageMaker Feature Store, you must first define and create the Feature Group schema specifying the RecordIdentifier and EventTime columns (2), then ingest feature records into the Feature Group via streaming or batch pipelines (1), and finally consume the records from the Online/Offline stores for inference and training (3). Architectural Deep Dive: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store provides a unified repository for ML features using Feature Groups: the Online Store delivers single-digit millisecond low-latency lookups for real-time inference (storing the latest record per ID), while the Offline Store appends historical records into an S3 Parquet catalog for training and Athena queries without training-serving skew. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option D is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario.
questions.use_case: FinTech fraud models ingest streaming card velocity features into a Feature Group enabled for both Online and Offline stores - serving live checkout endpoints in under 10 ms from the Online Store while data scientists build point-in-time accurate training sets from the Offline Store.
questions.hack: Sequence for Feature Store questions: 1) Create Feature Group -> 2) Ingest records (PutRecord / batch) -> 3) Query Online Store for real-time inference or Offline Store (Athena/S3) for training.

questions.stem: An ML engineer needs to use an ML model to predict the price of apartments in a specific location. Which metric should the ML engineer use to evaluate the model's performance?
options: Accuracy
Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)
F1 score
Mean absolute error (MAE)
questions.explanation: The correct choice is D: Option D (Mean absolute error (MAE)). For regression models, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) squares errors before averaging - heavily penalizing large outlier errors in the same units as the target variable - whereas Mean Absolute Error (MAE) weights all errors linearly (making it robust when outliers should not dominate), and R-Squared (R2) measures the proportion of variance explained by the model. Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option B is incorrect because this option either misapplies the AWS service outside its intended architectural pattern or violates the primary constraint (operational simplicity, cost efficiency, or target accuracy) specified in the scenario. Option C is incorrect because this option relies on standard Accuracy or fails to address minority class under-representation.
questions.use_case: Energy grid load forecasting models use RMSE because a single huge underestimation of peak megawatt demand causes a blackout, whereas retail house-price estimators with noisy billionaire mansions often track MAE/Median Absolute Error alongside RMSE.
questions.hack: Regression metric rule: Need to heavily penalize large outlier errors in target units? Pick RMSE. Want robustness against extreme outliers? Pick MAE.

questions.stem: An ML engineer has trained a neural network by using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The neural network performs poorly on the test set. The values for training loss and validation loss remain high and show an oscillating pattern. The values decrease for a few epochs and then increase for a few epochs before repeating the same cycle. What should the ML engineer do to improve the training process?
options: Introduce early stopping.
Increase the size of the test set.
Increase the learning rate.
Decrease the learning rate.
questions.explanation: The correct choice is D: Option D (Decrease the learning rate.). The learning rate controls the step size during gradient descent optimization: if the learning rate is too high, training loss oscillates wildly or diverges (fix by decreasing the learning rate); if it is too low, training converges painfully slowly or stalls in local minima (fix by increasing the learning rate or using a warm-up schedule). Why the distractors fail: Option A is incorrect because this option increases model complexity (adding more layers, neurons, or epochs) or reduces regularization, which worsens overfitting.
